# Bhūridattajātaka (Ja 543)

**ID:** Ja 543  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Bhūridattajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul5.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul5.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhūridattajātaka* (Ja 543), translated as *Bhuridatta the Wise*, is a major narrative work in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its opening setting, the Buddha recounted the story at Sāvatthī concerning lay devotees observing the fast-day. The core narrative relates that the Bodhisatta was reborn as the nāga prince Bhūridatta, who is captured and tormented by a snake charmer—the brahmin Ālambāyana—yet steadfastly endures his capture without using his powers against his captor, thereby exemplifying the perfection of moral conduct (*sīlapāramitā*) [Appleton 2010; Murphy 2010; Scheible 2011]. Winternitz observes that the work was likely an independent composition structured into eight sections (*khaṇḍas*), weaving together popular folklore concerning nāgas and garuḍas with Buddhist doctrinal debates [Winternitz 1933]. In particular, the text features stanzas criticizing brahmanical sacrificial practices, arguing against the veneration of fire (Agni) and water, and defending the Buddhist doctrine of karma [von Glasenapp 1966; Obeyesekere 2002; Alsdorf 1977].

Later Pali commentaries, including Dhammapāla’s *Paramatthadīpanī*, explicitly classify the *Bhūridattajātaka* as a locus classicus for the perfection of virtue [Scheible 2011]. The text has been widely depicted in Southeast Asian art, including 7th–12th-century Northeast Thai *sīmā* boundary stones that depict the brahmin Ālambāyana subduing the nāga, as well as 12th-century Burmese terracotta plaques [Murphy 2010; Ray 1946]. In Burma, the 15th-century poet-monk Raṭṭhasāra composed a noted metrical version of the story [Ray 1946]. In modern scholarship, Ludwig Alsdorf published an influential philological study examining its anti-brahmanical verses and proposing textual emendations [Alsdorf 1977; de Jong 1987].
